text: With the five requirements laid out, it's time to write real code. This lesson builds requirements two and three — translating a plain circuit spec into a QuantumCircuit, then running it both exactly and via shots.

build_circuit loops over the spec once, reads each tuple's first element as the gate name, and dispatches to the matching QuantumCircuit method. Only h and cx are handled, which is all the GHZ case needs, but the structure scales to arbitrarily complex specs without changing its core shape. Applied to the GHZ spec, this produces exactly the circuit you built by hand back in Chapter 2.

Before any measurement or shot-based noise enters the picture, Statevector computes the exact mathematical answer directly from the circuit's unitary operations — the exact amplitude for every one of the 8 basis states, with no sampling and no randomness. This is your ground truth for the comparison layer.

The shot-based layer needs its own copy of the circuit, because measurement is destructive — qc.copy() keeps the original, measurement-free circuit intact. Then it's the current post-2.0 pattern: transpile for the target backend, then run directly, with shots equal to 2048 controlling how many times the circuit gets sampled.

The GHZ circuit's exact answer is already established: amplitude 0.7071068 on both 000 and 111, exactly zero everywhere else, giving P(000) and P(111) at exactly 0.5 each. A real seeded run at 2048 shots gave something like 000: 1069, 111: 979, with all six other outcomes at exactly zero. Both fractions land reasonably close to 0.5, and critically, no counts at all appear on any outcome the exact statevector says should be impossible — the shape of a correctly working tool.
Next lesson builds the piece that decides, with actual statistics rather than a gut feeling, whether a disagreement like 1069 versus 1024 is ordinary noise or a genuine red flag.
